newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan gloomy about Peru hostage standoff.
newsitem.headline: Japan gloomy about Peru hostage standoff.

text.p: The prospects of winning the release of high-level hostages in Peru are now worse than at any time since leftist guerrillas seized the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima 17 days ago, a Japanese government spokesman said on Saturday.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto told a news briefing that talks between the Peruvian government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) were now at an impasse.
"The situation is more serious than ever before," he said. "It appears as if the incident will take a long time to resolve."
His remarks followed equally gloomy comments by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who said he was pessimistic about ending the standoff.
"I am not optimistic about the situation, seeing as the number of hostages has been reduced to a level where it is easy for the terrorists to control them," the premier told reporters.
The revolutionary group has 74 hostages, after releasing an estimated 430 captives in several waves. They stormed the residence during a December 17 party celebrating the birthday of Japan's emperor.
The remaining captives include more than a dozen Japanese businessmen, top Peruvian government officials and Fujimori's brother Pedro as well as Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki.
The MRTA is demanding the release of more than 400 comrades in Peruvian prisons.
Reflecting the apparent impasse, television coverage from the residence showed newly unfurled banners out of the windows calling on Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to negotiate.
"President Fujimori is only issuing tough statements, not opening dialogue...without dialogue there can be no solution," one of them read.
Japanese officials are still upset with Uruguay over its release of two suspected MRTA guerillas.
The move, ordered by a Uruguayan court, was followed within hours by the release of Uruguay's ambassador to Peru, who was among the dignitaries at the celebration.

Uruguayan Foreign Minister Alvaro Ramos told his Japanese opposite number Yukihiko Ikeda that Uruguay had not made any deal with the guerilla group. He was quoted as saying the freeing of the two alleged guerrillas "did not reflect the will of the government".
But the Japanese foreign ministry spokesman said the action had worsened the situation.
"We believe that the release of the Uruguay ambassador from the residence has complicated the hostage situation," he said.
About the only optimistic note coming from Japanese officials was that the living conditions for the hostages appeared to be good.

"According to the reports from those concerned and the interviews conducted inside the residence by the press, we feel the situation is calm... and their living conditions are improved," spokesman Hashimoto said.
Japan has been pushing for a peaceful end to the siege. The ambassador's residence is technically Japanese territory.
"The Japanese government is investing all its trust in Peru for a peaceful resolution to the incident," Hashimoto said.
